findings.text: The first paragraph tells a newcomer what Athena is, who it is for and what problem it solves, in plain words. The what and the why are covered before any detail.
findings.source: header lede: "Athena is an open-source system, written in Rust, that turns a short request into a change to a code repository... It solves the problem of AI edits that arrive unreviewed and unaccountable."

findings.text: The page explains why the address for Athena opens on a study of a different project, firstmate. Without this the switch would be confusing. Even so, nearly all of the page is about firstmate, so a newcomer who came to learn about Athena gets little about Athena past the header.
findings.source: header lede: "A study is Athena's written reading of another software project... Athena made this study of firstmate to show that it can read an unfamiliar project and explain it"

findings.text: The next step is linked near the top. The Next steps section gives a clear order: clone, check prerequisites, run ./setup.sh, then try `athena ask "add a changelog"`. A newcomer knows what to do next.
findings.source: header: "Next step: install Athena or read firstmate itself" and the Next steps section

findings.text: The page says Athena is written in Rust, but the prerequisites do not name a Rust toolchain. A newcomer can't tell whether setup.sh installs one or whether they need it already.
findings.source: Next steps: "have git 2.40 or later, a C linker, curl, and either Claude Code or npm"

findings.text: This link is for the project owner, but it sits in the header where every newcomer sees it. It has no explanation, so a first-time reader may wonder whether it applies to them.
findings.source: header: "Owner view: proposals waiting for your decision."

findings.text: The Start here section is well built. It defines terms first, gives a one-sentence answer to what firstmate is, and then walks through one task step by step. A newcomer can follow firstmate's basics from it.
findings.source: Start here: "The three parts below say what firstmate is, follow one piece of work, and say what happens when something fails"

findings.text: The States, Counters and Transitions sections go into exit codes, lock behavior and edge cases. Most newcomers don't need this depth, and it makes the page long. The early sections are still enough for a newcomer, and the depth does show how carefully Athena traces things.
findings.source: Transitions cards, e.g. t2: "the spawn is deferred with exit 75... lock contention or an unreadable capacity declaration refuses with exit 1"

findings.text: Several terms are openly marked as undefined in the source. That is honest, but it leaves a newcomer with unexplained words in the transition cards.
findings.source: Glossary: "endpoint — The firstmate source does not define an endpoint." (similarly captain call, durable record, heartbeat, wake)

findings.text: Every claim links to specific lines at a pinned commit. This shows Athena's main promise, traceability, in practice instead of only claiming it.
findings.source: Next steps: "Check a statement: follow a bracketed claim id to the claim, then its source link to the file and lines in firstmate at the pinned commit."
